source_text: Durat nempe inter vos Manichaeosque foedus, ut illi professione, vos argumentatione, primi quoque hominis naturam asseratis malam fuisse; quod licet totum ineptiarum mendaciorumque plenum esse (ut praetermissis sanctorum legionibus, primum post peccatum Adae iustitia arripiamus exemplum), Abelis sanctitate mirabili comprobatur, qui de peccatoribus natus, bene vivendi se non caruisse virtute, effectu quoque ipsius virtutis ostendit; verumtamen his praeteritis iuvat sententias Traducianae nationis urgere. Quale igitur autumas fuisse arbitrium liberum, quod collatum primis hominibus confiteris? Certe ut possent animi alternare motus, et vel facere malum, vel recedere a malo, vel deserere vel servare iustitiam. Voluntas ergo peccandi non fuisset, nisi volendi possibilitas anteisset. Hoc postquam uti coeperunt propria voluntate, id est motu animi cogente nullo, tu dicis liberum arbitrium perdidisse; quo quid potest furiosius cogitari? Ut enim vis argumenti tui expressa teneatur, dicis eam rem periisse propter voluntatem, quae data non est nisi propter voluntatem; peccatum quippe nihil est aliud quam voluntas mala; libertas autem ad hoc solum data est, ut voluntatem non cogeret, sed permitteret exoriri; hanc autem tu libertatem conditionem suam dicis voluntatis opere perdidisse, ut per hoc interiisse credatur, per quod solum probatur vigere. Voluntas ergo mala non quidem fructus, sed testimonium libertatis est. Libertas autem nihil est aliud quam possibilitas boni malique, sed voluntarii. Qui ergo fieri potuit ut per hoc interiret, per quod proditur instituta, cum mala voluntas et bona voluntas non exitia sint, sed praeconia libertatis? Ac per hoc quantum distat inter officia atque discrimina, tantum inter opinionem tuam et rationem arbitrii liberi, cui excidium putas de suis laudibus comparatum. Quid ergo novum, quid insperatum delinquente homine accidit, per quod Dei instituta corruerent? Factus est qui peccare et non peccare posset; cum peccavit, fecit quod non debuit quidem, sed potuit tamen; per quid igitur facultatem illam perderet, quae ad hoc fuerat instituta, ut posset velle, posset nolle quod voluit.
pass_a_gloss: A treaty indeed lasts between you and the Manichaeans, that they by profession, you by argumentation, assert that the nature even of the first human was evil; which although the whole is full of ineptitudes and lies (that, the legions of the holy having been omitted, we may first snatch after Adam's sin an example of justice), is proved by Abel's wonderful holiness, who born from sinners shows by the effect also of the virtue itself that he did not lack the virtue of living well; nevertheless these things having been passed it pleases to press the sentences of the Traducian nation. Of what sort therefore do you assert that free decision was, which you confess was conferred on the first humans? Certainly that they could alternate the motions of the mind, and either do evil, or recede from evil, or desert or keep justice. A will of sinning therefore would not have been, unless a possibility of willing had gone before. This after they began to use by their own will, that is by a motion of the mind no one compelling, you say free decision lost; than which what more furious can be thought? For that the force of your argument may be held expressed, you say that thing perished on account of will, which was not given except on account of will; for sin is nothing other than an evil will; but freedom was given for this alone, that it would not compel a will, but would permit it to arise; but you say this freedom lost its own condition by a work of will, so that it is believed to have perished through that through which alone it is proved to thrive. An evil will therefore is not indeed a fruit, but a testimony of freedom. But freedom is nothing other than a possibility of good and of evil, but of the voluntary. How therefore could it be done that it would perish through that through which it is betrayed instituted, when an evil will and a good will are not destructions, but proclamations of freedom? And through this as much as there is a distance between offices and discriminations, so much between your opinion and the reason of free decision, for which you think destruction was furnished from its own praises. What therefore new, what unhoped happened with the human offending, through which God's institutions would collapse? He was made who could sin and not sin; when he sinned, he did what he ought not indeed, but nevertheless could; through what therefore would he lose that faculty, which had been instituted for this, that he could will, could be unwilling what he willed.

pass_b_english: The alliance between you and the Manichaeans plainly endures: they by open profession and you by argument maintain that even the first human’s nature was evil. All this is full of absurdities and lies. Passing over the legions of saints, let us take the first example of righteousness after Adam’s sin: Abel’s wonderful holiness proves it. Born from sinners, he showed through the actual exercise of virtue that he did not lack the power to live well (Genesis 4:4; Hebrews 11:4). Yet, leaving these examples aside, it is useful to press the pronouncements of the party teaching inherited sin.

What do you suppose the free will you acknowledge was given to the first humans was like? Surely it meant they could change their minds: do evil or withdraw from evil, abandon or keep justice. There would therefore have been no will to sin unless the capacity to will came first. You say that after they began using their own will—that is, a movement of mind compelled by no one—they lost free will. What could be imagined more insane?

To state your argument’s force precisely: you say that what was given only for the sake of willing perished because of willing. Sin is simply an evil will. Freedom was given solely to permit the will to arise, not to compel it. Yet you say this freedom lost its condition through an act of will, so it is believed to have died through the very thing that alone proves it alive. An evil will is therefore not freedom’s fruit, but evidence of freedom. Freedom is simply the capacity for good and evil, provided they are voluntary. How, then, could it perish through the very thing for which it is shown to have been instituted, when an evil will and a good will are not freedom’s destruction but its witnesses?

The distance between proper functions and destructive crises is therefore the distance between your opinion and the meaning of free will, whose destruction you think was supplied by its own grounds for praise. What new or unforeseen thing happened when humanity sinned, to overthrow God’s arrangements? A being was made who could sin and not sin. When he sinned, he did what he ought not to have done, but what he nevertheless could do. How, then, would he lose that capacity, instituted precisely so that he could will something and could refuse what he willed (Genesis 4:4) (Hebrews 11:4)?

choices.why: Julian's polemic target is inherited sin as a natural evil (malum naturale), the vine-layer metaphor, not a later systematic 'original sin' slogan and not soul-traducianism as such.
rejected: original sin (later system as default gloss)
traducianism of the soul (not the load here)

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
